title: Utah replaced the winningest coach in school history. It’s having its best season in 2 decades
content:
SALT LAKE CITY — Morgan Scalley needed to keep his quarterback. Devon Dampier had followed offensive coordinator Jason Beck to Utah from New Mexico, and when Beck followed Kyle Whittingham to Michigan last December, Dampier had options.

So Scalley made his way to Dampier’s home in Salt Lake City.

He apologized to Dampier for what was happening. Scalley felt he deserved an apology. But Scalley spent the next 45 minutes selling Dampier on his vision for Utah as he moved up from defensive coordinator to head coach.

He told Dampier he was going to find a coordinator who fit Dampier’s dual-threat game instead of trying to fit Dampier’s game into a new system. He was going to build the offense around his quarterback and wanted one who was physical, but creative and flexible, capable of moving the ball different ways.

“That was huge to hear from your head coach. That amount of belief and considering you in that decision is pretty significant. That was the main reason (I stayed),” Dampier said. “That was all I needed to hear.”

The program Scalley took over Dec. 13 changed dramatically two weeks later when Whittingham replaced Sherrone Moore at Michigan. Whittingham had been at Utah 32 years, only a handful of seasons longer than Scalley, who arrived as a player in 2001 and never left, joining the administration in 2006 and Whittingham’s staff a year later.

After the 2025 season, Utah’s administration pushed Whittingham — the program’s winningest coach ever — to step aside and let Scalley, labeled the coach-in-waiting, take over the program.

Scalley inherited a 10-win program capable of winning the Big 12. But Whittingham coaxed six coaches and the strength and conditioning coach to join him in Ann Arbor. He made Beck the nation’s highest-paid offensive coordinator. All-American edge rusher John Henry Daley and tight end J.J. Buchanan were among a handful of players to follow him.

“I don’t think I had enough time to feel sorry for myself. It was just happening so fast,” Scalley said. “And I truly believed in this place.”

Scalley saw an opportunity to make the program his own. He had no choice but to put his fingerprints all over it; Whittingham’s were largely gone.

“It was fortunate for me that he actually took some people so that it could be my team, as opposed to guys are left over and, ‘Oh, now a new way of doing things,'” Scalley said.

Eleven months after Scalley’s promotion, he and Utah are 9-0, ranked No. 2 and positioned to make the Utes’ first College Football Playoff. They’re one of two programs yet to lose. They are playing a brand of football that reflects Scalley’s long-standing “RSNB” motto: Relentless, Smart, Nasty Ballhawks.

Whittingham and Michigan are 5-4. Last week, Whittingham fired Beck. Questions persist about the Wolverines’ trajectory.

As Scalley watches that season play out, his mind largely drifts to the coaches’ families, on whom losing can take a toll as a community’s anger rises.

Scalley said he and Whittingham text periodically during the offseason. When Scalley thinks about him, he mostly feels gratitude.

“He gave me every opportunity along the way,” he said. “I love him. I’ll always love him.”

Scalley had an advantage over most other first-year hires as Utah’s coach-in-waiting. He built his own program in his mind long before he could make it a reality. He had a list of coaches he knew he’d call. That included offensive coordinator Kevin McGiven, hired from Utah State.

McGiven has gotten the best out of Dampier, who has the fourth-best odds to win the Heisman Trophy. Utah is 13th this season in yards per play, up from 18th in 2025. And McGiven has found ways to use speedy backup quarterback Byrd Ficklin. Utah will often play both quarterbacks at once, leaving defenses guessing at what’s coming. The Utes have played Dampier and Ficklin together on 78 snaps, more than any other team in the country has played two quarterbacks on the same play.

Scalley reshaped Utah’s strength and conditioning program, turning to Steve Saunders, who had mostly coached in the NFL and initially came to Utah in a supporting role on staff.

“I just felt like we needed to be more cutting edge,” Scalley said. “I wanted the way we lifted and conditioned to be much more position specific, and I wanted the functionality of that to make us better football players, not better weight lifters.”

He also embraced sports science and tracking players’ bodies, molding practice and lifting plans around what the data told him.

He cut aerobic training and embraced anaerobic training instead, focused on explosiveness and burst. Utah doesn’t run gassers.

“53 yards down, 53 yards back. No sprint, no burst. When does that happen in football? Never. But people do it,” he said.

He loved the culture he inherited but found it was largely split between offense and defense. He wanted the whole team and staff on the same page. As he built his staff, he focused on coaches who thrived as teachers.

Scalley said he leans on Stoic ideas learned in reading authors such as Ryan Holiday, whose books “Ego is the Enemy” and “Stillness is the Key” were influential in shaping his own philosophy. He had his staff listen to an hourlong keynote speech from Tim Kight, who coached under Urban Meyer and later became a speaker on leadership.

The general idea was building a mental toughness, a consistency and the ability to find any road possible to maximize the performance of everyone inside the program.

When Scalley was DC, “RSNB” was the defense’s signature moniker. Linebacker Trey Reynolds first heard it on one of his first recruiting calls with Colton Swan, who coached linebackers under Whittingham and was promoted to defensive coordinator under Scalley.

As head coach, Scalley expanded “Relentless, Smart, Nasty, Ballhawks” to define the whole team. Scalley often mentions players owning the 20 square feet around them in every minute of every day.

“Everyone talks the same language,” safety Nate Ritchie said. “I think it brings in a greater sense of unison and bond with the guys that are in the building.”

Scalley wanted to run his program with humility and make the process collaborative.

In a recent film session, he pressed defensive ends coach Inoke Breckterfield on how he should coach the ends to defend zone-read plays when they knew the quarterback would decide whether to keep the ball or hand off. Should they storm up field? Should they charge the mesh point? Should they use a step-shuffle technique?

“What do you want?” Breckterfield asked.

Scalley pressed him. No, what would Breckterfield do?

He said he wants to listen. He wants to empower his coaches without micromanaging them. He gave up calling the defense and handed it to Swan, who’d never done it.

“In our profession, people have too many egos. I want to know where my blind spots are. I wanna know where I’m weak, where I can get better,” Scalley said. “And I want coaches that are the same way, that don’t get butthurt when you tell them, ‘Hey, you need to change this up.'”

As for his roster, Scalley worked to forge connections during the offseason. The two words that come up most often when players talk about him? Energy and consistency.

“He’s a very open guy. He always says if you have questions, come talk to me,” said Ritchie, who worked with Scalley as his position coach when he was also the coordinator and snatched the game-sealing interception in Saturday’s Holy War win over BYU. “He’s always looking for ways to get better, looking for feedback and really wants to connect on an individual level. He’s not going to scream and yell. He’s going to have a conversation and get to know you.”

The team’s 12-person leadership council can push back on coaches in a more collaborative process. Scalley still has final word, but players say it helps them feel more heard and understood than in the past.

“Scalley’s a little more in tune with us players. He allows us to have a bigger voice than we might have had last year on how our bodies are feeling, how we think something should work or if we think practice should be shorter,” Dampier said. “If he says no, there’s a reason. It’s not, ‘We’re having a longer practice to have a longer practice.’ He’s very transparent.”

Dampier gets around campus on an Airwheel motorized scooter, essentially a piece of carry-on luggage that doubles as a seat with handlebars to steer. He discovered it on TikTok during preseason camp and thought it would make traversing campus easier and take wear and tear off his legs. After he showed up to the facility with it, Scalley bought one of his own.

Initially, people thought Scalley had swiped Dampier’s scooter. But he’d made good on his promise days earlier to buy one, a comment Dampier took as a joke.

The team’s connection has added up to a breakthrough season.

“We could tell in spring ball that we had something special,” Reynolds said. “Coach Scalley said it, the leaders said it. The team was saying all the time, we have something special here.”

Early in spring, before the team had even donned pads, junior cornerback James Chenault Jr., better known as Bobo, warned his teammates if he picked off a pass later in practice, he was throwing the ball in the air. They needed to celebrate with him.

He did nab an interception. He threw it up and sparked a party on the defensive sideline. Reynolds saw the joy on his teammates’ faces. It looked and felt different to him. Chenault won, sure. But the team won. Every defender seemed to recognize it.

“That was a moment where it was like, man, we’re a team. We love each other. We love the success of everyone around us,” Reynolds said. “That was the start of it all. Since then, we celebrate together. We love each other up when we make big plays and help each other up when we make mistakes.”

The Utes hadn’t been 9-0 since 2008, when they were in the Mountain West and capped the season with a 31-17 upset win over Nick Saban and Alabama in the Sugar Bowl. They’re behind only Georgia in the Playoff rankings. They’re alone in first place in the Big 12, aiming for the program’s first conference title since it won the Pac-12 in 2022. Dampier could be Utah’s first Heisman finalist since Alex Smith in 2004.

So much of the conversation around Utah this offseason centered around what it lost.

Those who stayed reshaped the narrative.
